title: Peace walks
hook: Maha Ghosananda leads peace walks across Cambodia after the killing years

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tenzin Gyatso, a monk in maroon who calls kindness his practice. Your line: kindness as practice.

A dirt road in Cambodia. At the front, a small, elderly monk in saffron, walking slowly, sometimes smiling, sometimes sprinkling water from a bowl on the people who kneel by the road. Behind him, a long line: monks, nuns, laypeople, some carrying flags, some barefoot. The fields they pass have seen terrible things; in some places there are still mines in the ground. Nobody in the line is armed. They're walking through a country torn apart by its own government, and they're walking for peace.
screen: `A DIRT ROAD, A SMALL MONK.` → `A LONG LINE BEHIND HIM.` → `NO ONE ARMED.`

segments.voice: His name was Maha Ghosananda, a Cambodian monk, and he was living abroad when the Khmer Rouge came to power. Under that regime, temples were emptied, monks were killed or forced out of their robes, and Cambodians died in the fields and in the prisons. His students say his own family was among those lost. When the killing years ended, he went to the refugee camps along the Thai border and set up simple temples among the tents. There, people say, he chanted one verse from the Dhammapada again and again. In Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." He said it to people who had lost everything to hatred. Not to excuse what happened, but because, as he saw it, more hatred would only start the circle again. Later, back in Cambodia, he began leading walks for peace, the Dhammayietra, a pilgrimage of the Dhamma, through regions where fighting hadn't fully stopped. People came out of their villages to meet the walkers with water and incense. Some walkers were hurt along the way. Still they walked. His way of putting it was plain: peace is made step by step, slowly, the way you walk. Each step can be a kind of meditation, and each meditation a step toward peace. He didn't promise it would be quick. He promised it would be walked.
screen: `THE KILLING YEARS.` · `CHANTING IN THE REFUGEE CAMPS.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE DHAMMAYIETRA: WALKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and take one unhurried step, then another, at the pace of someone in a long line; if you're seated, press each foot gently into the floor in turn. Let one quiet word ride along with each step: peace, not as a demand, more like company. If your mind runs ahead to your list, come back to the next step; there's nowhere to arrive.
Peace walks. The Dhammayietra, Maha Ghosananda's walks through a wounded Cambodia, made one slow step at a time.
Your line: step by step, peace. Hatred ceases by love, one step at a time. Day one thousand twenty-one, done.

howItsDone: In Cambodia, the Dhammayietra peace walks continued after Maha Ghosananda, and Buddhists elsewhere practice walking meditation, sometimes walking together in silence for peace.

original.note: Pali averena, 'by non-hatred', from the Dhammapada verse Müller renders 'hatred ceases by love'.

chat.says: After so much killing, how could a monk tell survivors to stop hating?
options: He chanted that hatred never ends hatred; more of it only starts the circle again.
He told them what happened didn't matter, and they should simply forget it.
He told them to hate only the leaders, since well-aimed hatred brings peace.
chat.meaning: Maha Ghosananda chanted Dhammapada 5: hatred ceases by love. He didn't excuse what happened; he saw that more hatred would only start the circle again.

notes: Müller 1881 Dhammapada v.5 quoted in part: 'For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.' Confirm exact punctuation of the quoted portion.

'Step by step' echoes Maha Ghosananda's own teaching (and the title of a modern, copyrighted collection); paraphrased only.
